## Methods

Mice housing
All animal studies received ethical approval and were approved by the Ministry of Environment and Agriculture Denmark (Miljø- og Fødevarestyrelsen), under license 2023-15-0201-01544. All mice were housed under a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle in a temperature-controlled (22°C) and humidity-controlled facility that had ad libitum access to diets and drinking water. 4-week-old C57BL/6J male mice (Janvier Labs) were fed with a chow diet (NIH-31, Zeigler Brothers Inc., 8% calories from fat) for 2 weeks of acclimatization and then were fed with either a low-fat diet (LF, D12450J, 10% kcal from fat, Research Diet) or a high-fat diet (HF, D12492, 60% kcal from fat, Research Diet) for 9 weeks. After 9 weeks of feeding, half of the HF-fed mice were randomly assigned to the diet regression group, which was given LFD. LFD is carefully chosen to match the food source (animal vs plant) and the micronutrient composition of HFD.

Mouse husbandry
All male virgin mice were maintained on the assigned diet until 21 weeks of age and mated with 10-week-old C57BL/6J female virgin mice (Janvier Labs). 8-week-old C57BL/6J female mice were fed with a chow diet for 2 weeks of acclimatization and then were fed with LF during breeding and lactation. Mating was set up for 5 days in a female’s cage, and vaginal plugs were checked every morning. All mice, including the F0 HF group, were maintained on LF during breeding to remove confounding effects from maternal diets. Males were sent from breeding cages to the original cage to be fed with the assigned diet for an additional 2 weeks and then sacrificed. The offspring from all groups of founders consumed only LF. Representative male offspring from six litters per group were included in all analyses.

Intraperitoneal glucose and insulin tolerance tests
Mice were fasted for 6 h for glucose-tolerance tests. Fasting glucose levels were measured, and then mice were intraperitoneally injected with 2 g/kg body weight of 20% glucose solution (B. Braun Medical A/S). For intraperitoneal insulin-tolerance tests, random-fed glucose levels were measured, and mice were intraperitoneally injected with 0.75 IU/kg body weight of 100 IU stock insulin (Novo Nordisk). Blood glucose levels were measured at 15, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min after injecting glucose or insulin using a CONTOUR®NEXT glucometer (Bayer). For ipGTT/ipITT, we omitted mice with strongly delayed rises in glucose and no discernible drop in blood glucose, respectively, from analyses, as this was the consequence of mal injection outside the peritoneum. For area under the curve (AUC) calculations, we have normalized serum [Glu] values to [Glu, T0] of each animal to account for intra-animal variability in glucose responses and relative glucose responses.

Tissue collection
Mice were sacrificed by carbon dioxide euthanasia. Livers, eWAT, iWAT and BAT were weighed, snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored in −80°C. Pieces from liver and eWAT were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for histology analysis. For serum collection, blood collected by the cardiac puncture was centrifuged at 2000×g for 15 min. The supernatant was collected and stored in −80°C.

Sperm collection
The prospective intervention study complies with relevant ethical regulations and was conducted between May 2020 and April 2022 at the Fertility Clinic, Zealand University Hospital, Denmark. The study was approved by the Danish National Committee on Health Research Ethics (SJ-769), the Danish Data Protection Agency (REG-048-2019) and registered on the Clinical Trial website (www.ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT04721938). The primary outcomes have been published77. Briefly, mature sperm cells were collected from the cauda epididymis. Sperm cells are allowed to swim out from the cauda epididymis and incubate in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at 37°C for 15 min. Supernatant containing sperms was passed through a 40-µm cell strainer and incubated in a somatic cell lysis buffer (0.5% Triton-X and 0.1% SDS) for 40 min on ice. Sperms were centrifuged at 600×g for 5 min and pellets were washed with PBS and pelted again at 600×g for 5 min. The supernatant was discarded, and the pellets were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80°C.

Zygotic miRNA microinjection and embryo implantation
Ovulation of prepubescent (4-week-old) C57BL/6J females was induced by intraperitoneal (IP) injection of PMSG, 5 IU/female, followed by IP injection of hCG, 5 IU/female, 47 h later. After the second injection, females were set in breeding with C57BL/6J stud males. The next morning, they were monitored for the formation of a vaginal plug (indicating mating had occurred during the night). Females were euthanized and oviducts were dissected to harvest the cumuli containing zygotes and unfertilized oocytes. Cumuli were disaggregated by incubation in a 10 mg/ml solution of Hyaluronidase (Sigma-Aldrich ref. H4272) in M2 medium (Sigma-Aldrich ref. M7167) at RT for 10 minutes. Zygotes were sorted out, assessed by the presence of the second polar body and cultured in KSOM medium (Merck Millipore ref. MR-106-D). Oocytes were discarded. Each miRNA was diluted at 10 ng/ul in microinjection buffer (5 mM Tris, 0.1 mM EDTA, pH 7.4) as a stock solution and kept at −80°C. The day of microinjection, 1.5 ng/ul solutions were prepared from the stock, and injected in the pronuclei of the zygotes following standard microinjection procedures. miRIDIAN mimics were ordered from Dharmacon: Inert miRNA control is based on C. elegans cel-mir-67, which is not expressed in mouse or human cells (5‘-UCACAACCUCCUAGAAAGAGUAGA-3‘, cat. no. CN-001000-01-05), mmu-let-7d-5p (cat. no. C-310486-07-0002) and mmu-let-7e-5p (cat. no. C-310507-07-0005). Injected zygotes were cultured in KSOM until the microinjection session was completed and then cryopreserved by the “Slow Freezing” Method (Manipulating the Mouse Embryo, a Laboratory Manual, fourth edition, Chapter 16, Richard Behringer et al. Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press, 2014) and transported to SDU at −150°C for embryo transfer and recovery.

The frozen microinjected embryos were thawed at SDU and cultured in KSOM (Merck, MR-121-D) for 40 minutes (Manipulating the Mouse Embryo, a Laboratory Manual, fourth edition, Chapter 16, Richard Behringer et al. Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press, 2014). Viable embryos with intact zona pellucida were selected for further transfer. These embryos were then washed in 10 drops of M2 and surgically transferred to the oviducts of 0.5 dpc pseudo-pregnant females. Pseudopregnancy was induced in the females by mating them with a vasectomized male. Prior to implantation, the pseudopregnant females were anesthetized with ketamine (100 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg) through intraperitoneal injection, and the surgical embryo transfer procedure was performed following the protocol described by Behringer et al. (Manipulating the Mouse Embryo, a Laboratory Manual, fourth edition, Chapter 6, Richard Behringer Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Press, 2014). Postoperative analgesic treatment with carprofen (5 mg/kg) was administered subcutaneously for 48 hours.

8-cell-morula blastomere disaggregation
miRNAs were injected into the embryo at the zygote stage as described above. After injection, embryos were incubated in KSOM (KSOM-Embryomax advanced embryo medium, Merck Millipore #MD-101-D) for 48-56 hours at 37°C, in 5% C02. The culture medium was refreshed daily. In the afternoon of the third day of culture, when the embryos had reached the 8-cell morula stage, they were incubated at RT in Tyrod’s solution (Sigma-Aldrich T1788) for up to 30 seconds until the zona pellucida was completely dissolved. Afterwards, the naked morulae were washed through three drops of M2 medium (Sigma-Aldrich M7167) and finally incubated in KSOM without Ca2+ and Mg2+ at RT for 20 minutes. Then, embryos were moved to a new drop of fresh M2 medium and there, pipetted up and down repeatedly to facilitate the blastomere disaggregation. When single blastomeres were obtained, they were individually transferred to single wells of a 96-well single-cell-sequencing plate from VWR (Cat. No. 82006-636) with 2 μl of RNAse inhibitor mix (containing 0.12 μl Triton-X-100 10%, 0.1 μl RNAse inhibitor (Takara (Cat. No. 2313B, 40 U/μl), 1.78 μl MilliQ water (RNAse-free)). Plates were then frozen at −80°C until the sequencing was performed.

Lipidomics and metabolomics
Serum extraction. 100 µL of serum was mixed with 1000 µL of a 2:1 chloroform/methanol solution and 200 µL of water. Four blank samples, each containing 100 µL of water, were processed in parallel. The mixtures were shaken at 1000 rpm for 30 minutes at 4°C, followed by centrifugation at 16,000×g for 10 minutes at 4°C to separate the phases. The aqueous phase was re-extracted with 350 µL of an 86:14:1 chloroform/methanol/water solution. The organic phase from this re-extraction was combined with the corresponding organic phase from the initial extraction. The aqueous fraction was dried using SpeedVac, while the organic phase was dried under a stream of nitrogen. For subsequent analysis, the dried aqueous fractions were reconstituted in 30 µL of 1% formic acid for metabolomics. The organic phase was reconstituted in 30 µL of lipidomic solvent A (5:1:4 isopropanol/methanol/water with 5 mM ammonium acetate and 0.1% acetic acid). A pooled quality control sample was prepared for each analytical setup by combining 5 µL from each sample, excluding blanks.

Lipidomics analysis. For lipidomics analysis, 2.5 µL of each sample was injected into an Agilent 1290 Infinity UPLC system (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) equipped with a Zorbax Eclipse Plus C18 guard column (2.1×5 mm, 1.8 µm) and an analytical column (2.1×150 mm, 1.8 µm), maintained at 50°C. Analytes were eluted at a flow rate of 400 µL/min using eluent A (water with 5 mM ammonium acetate and 0.1% acetic acid) and eluent B (99:1 isopropanol/water with 5 mM ammonium acetate and 0.1% acetic acid). The gradient was as follows: 0% B from 0 to 1 min, 0–25% B from 1 to 1.5 min, 25–95% B from 1.5 to 12 min, 95% B from 12 to 14 min, and 95-0% B from 14 to 15 min, followed by a 3-minute equilibration. For metabolomics analysis, 1.5 µL of each sample was injected into the same UPLC-MS system, but with a ZORBAX Eclipse Plus C18 guard column (2.1×50 mm, 1.8 µm) and an analytical column (2.1×150 mm, 1.8 µm) maintained at 40°C. Eluent A was 0.1% formic acid, and eluent B was 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile. The gradient was as follows: 3% B from 0 to 1.5 min, 3–40% B from 1.5 to 4.5 min, 40–95% B from 4.5 to 7.5 min, 95% B from 7.5 to 10.1 min, and 95–3% B from 10.1 to 10.5 min, followed by a 3.5-minute equilibration. Both analyses were performed on a 6530B quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometer (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) for mass spectrometric detection in positive and negative ion modes. MS1 mode settings included a scanning range of 50–1700 m/z for lipidomic and 10-1050 m/z for metabolomics, with 2 scans/sec. Internal calibration was performed using Hexakis (1H,1H,3H-tetrafluoropropoxy) phosphazene delivered through a second needle in the ion source via an isocratic pump running at 20 µL/min. An iterative data-dependent MS2 mode was used for fragmentation in both analyses, with the following settings: collision energy at 40 V (lipidomics) and 20-40 V (metabolomics), precursor threshold at 5000 counts, and active exclusion after 2 spectra, with re-inclusion after 0.5 min.

Data processing and normalization. All data was converted .mzML format using ProteoWizard83. Lipidomics data were annotated in MS-Dial (v. 4.9) against the incorporated lipid-blast84 with an MS1/MS2 mass tolerance of 0.005/0.01 Da and a minimum identification score of 70%. The annotated compounds were exported to PCDL manager B.08.00 (Agilent Technologies) to create a database for area extraction in Profinder 10.0 (Agilent Technologies). Metabolomics data were processed in MzMine (v2.59) utilizing modules such as ADAP chromatogram builder and deconvolution. Compounds were annotated at Metabolomics Standards Initiative (MSI) levels 3 using the libraries of National Institute of Standards and Technology 2017 (NIST17) and MassBank of North America (MoNa). Features with signals less than 5 times those in blanks or missing in more than 20% of QC samples were removed, and signals were QC corrected using statTarget85.

Data analysis. For metabolomics pathway enrichment analysis (KEGG pathways of Mus musculus), comparing F0 LF and F0 HF serum (parameters 'Scatter plot', 'Hypergeometric test', 'relative-betweenness Centrality', 'Use all compounds in the selected pathway library') of differentially abundant polar metabolites (p ≤ 0.1) were loaded into Metaboanalyst 6.0. For lipidomics and metabolomics, principal component analysis and heatmap representation of an indicated number of differentially abundant lipids and metabolites were generated using 'Statistical Feature' (one-factor option), Sample normalization=' Normalization by sum', Data transformation='Log transformation (base 10)' and Data scaling='Mean Centring'.

Serum insulin and leptin ELISA. Serum insulin and leptin levels were measured by mouse insulin ELISA kit (Mercodia, Uppsala, Sweden) and mouse leptin ELISA kit (Crystal Chem, IL, USA) according to manufactures’ protocol.

Histology and staining. Liver and adipose tissues fixed with 4% of PFA were used for histology analyses. Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissues were cut into 3 μm sections. Sections were stained by haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Sirius Red by standard procedures at the Department of Pathology at Odense University Hospital, Odense, Denmark. Immunohistochemistry for CD45 was performed on Ventana BenchMark Ultra (Roche) with ready-to-use CD45 (LCA) (2B11 & PD7/26) Mouse Monoclonal Antibody.

A liver pathologist (SD) assigned steatosis, lobular inflammation, ballooning, fibrosis stage, and portal inflammation. Steatosis was graded as S0 (<5% hepatocytes with large fat vacuoles), S1 (5–33%), S2 (>33–66%), and S3 (>66% hepatocytes with large fat vacuoles)86. Lobular inflammation (0-3) and hepatocellular ballooning (0-2) were assessed according to the NAS-CRN Activity Score by Kleiner et al.86. Also, portal inflammation was assessed, using a 4-tiered score by Kleine et al. Liver fibrosis stage was assessed according to NAS-CRN for fibrosis; F-0, no fibrosis; F-1, perisinusoidal or periportal fibrosis; F-2, perisinusoidal and portal/periportal fibrosis; F-3, bridging fibrosis; F-4, cirrhosis.

Measurement of adipocyte volumes. The volume weighted mean volume of adipocytes was determined from the H&E sections with newCAST stereology software (Visiopharm), autodisector; measurements on systematic, randomly selected fields from 6 mice of all F0 and F1 groups were performed on at least 75 adipocyte profiles in each tissue.

Proteomics from epididymal white adipose tissue. Deep frozen fat pads (200 mg of epididymal adipose tissue) were powdered with a mortar-pestle and subjected to homogenization with ceramic beads (Percellys, 5500 rpm, 2×10 seconds, 30 seconds break) in the buffer containing 50 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 1% Triton-X-100, 100 mM NaF, 10 mM sodium orthovanadate, 10 mM EDTA, 0.2% SDS, 100 mM NaCl. Tissue homogenates were further processed to remove the nucleic acid traces (Diagenode SA; 10 min, cycle 30/30 seconds, at 4°C). Floating fat and tissue debris were removed from protein extracts by centrifugation at 20,000×g. 150 mg of proteins were precipitated with 4x volume of ice-cold acetone and washed with ice-cold acetone twice. Air-dry pellets were resuspended in 8 M Urea/50 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TAEB) buffer supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail (Sigma). 50 mg of the samples were incubated with 5 mM dithiothreitol at 25°C for 60 min, followed by treatment with 40 mM chloroacetamide for 30 min (room temperature, light-protected). Lys-C protease (enzyme: substrate ratio of 1:75) was added for 4 hours at 25°C. The TAEB-diluted sample (2 M Urea final) was supplemented with trypsin (1:75 ratio) followed by overnight digestion at 25°C. Acidified peptides (1% formic acid final) were purified on the SDR-RP (C18) multi-stop-and-go-tip (StageTip)87.

LC MS/MS label-free quantitative proteomic analysis from epididymal white adipose tissue. All samples were analyzed by the Proteomics Facility on a Q Exactive Plus Orbitrap mass spectrometer coupled to an EASY nLC 1000 (Thermo Scientific). Peptides were loaded with solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) onto an in-house packed analytical column (50 cm – 75 µm I.D., filled with 2.7 µm Poroshell EC120 C18, Agilent) and separated with 150 min gradients. Peptides were chromatographically separated at a constant flow rate of 250 nL/min using the following gradient: 4–6% solvent B (0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile) within 5.0 min, 6–23% solvent B within 120.0 min, 23–54% solvent B within 7.0 min, 54–85% solvent B within 6.0 min, followed by washing and column equilibration. The mass spectrometer was operated in data-dependent acquisition mode. The MS1 survey scan was acquired from 300–1750 m/z at a resolution of 70,000. The top 10 most abundant peptides were isolated within a 2.1 Th window and subjected to HCD fragmentation at a normalized collision energy of 27%. The AGC target was set to 5E5 charges, allowing a maximum injection time of 60 ms. Productions were detected in the Orbitrap at a resolution of 17,500. Precursors were dynamically excluded for 20.0 s. All mass spectrometric raw data were processed with MaxQuant88 (version 1.5.3.8, using default parameters and searched against the canonical murine Uniprot reference proteome (UP589, downloaded on 28/08/2020). Label-free quantification option was enabled, as was the match-between-runs option between replicates. Follow-up analysis was done in Perseus89 1.6.15. Hits from the decoy database, the contaminant list, and those only identified by modified peptides were removed. Afterwards, results were filtered for data completeness in replicate groups, and LFQ values were imputed using sigma downshift with standard settings. Finally, FDR-controlled T-tests between sample groups were performed with s0=0.2. Proteins were annotated on GOBP, GOCC, KEGG and Pfam terms. Afterwards, all one-way ANOVA (s=0.2) significant candidates were Z-scored and hierarchically clustered using the Euclidean distance model. Resulting clusters were merged onto the whole dataset, and a Fisher's Exact Test was calculated on cluster level with the whole dataset as background.

RNA isolation from mouse tissue and primary adipocytes. Total RNAs from tissues, sperm, and primary adipocytes were isolated using the TRI reagent (Sigma) followed by clean-up with RPE buffer (Qiagen, Germany). The quality of RNA was validated by the Agilent RNA 6000 Nano-Kit in Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer according to the manufacturer’s protocol. (Agilent Technologies, Waldbronn, Germany).

RNA sequencing. Small RNA sequencing: (1) For sRNA-seq from F0 sperm, library preparation and sRNA-seq were performed at Cologne Centre for Genomics, Germany. 50 ng of total RNA was used for library preparation, followed by size selection (Small RNA-Seq Library Prep Kit, Lexogen). The library was sequenced in 1×50-bp single-end reads on NovaSeq 6000 serie no. A00316. (2) Small RNA sequencing from F0 and F1 eWAT was carried out after quality control, 125 ng of total RNA was used for library preparation (Nextflex library kit), followed by sequencing by 1×50-bp single-end reads on Illumina Novaseq 6000. mRNA sequencing: mRNA sequencing was performed in-house. After quality control, 1 µg of total RNA was used for library preparation (NEBNext RNA prep kit) followed by 2×50 bp paired-end sequencing on Illumina Novaseq 6000.

RNA seq data analysis
Small RNA sequencing of spermatozoa. SncRNA-seq analysis of murine sperm was performed with Seqpac ver. 1.2.0, where sncRNA biotypes were annotated with 1 mismatch against Ensembl protein and non-coding RNA from GRCm39, miRbase, piRNA from piRBase ver. 3.0, tRNA from tRNAscan-SE, rRNA from RNAcentral and mitochondria from GRCm39:MT. Biotypes were assessed based on the following hierarchy: miRNAs, mitochondrial rRNAs, rRNAs, mitochondrial protein-coding mRNAs, mitochondrial tRNAs, tRNAs, piRNAs, nuclear protein-coding mRNAs, lncRNAs, and miscRNAs. Baseline filtering of one read per sample, and a size of 15–75 nt long was performed. Normalization was performed with counts per million (cpm).

Small RNA sequencing of somatic (adipose) tissue. Adapter sequences were trimmed from raw miRNA-seq reads using Cutadapt. The processed reads were mapped to the reference genome and aligned using the Bowtie algorithm within the miRDeep2 pipeline90. Normalization was performed using the Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM) method to account for sequencing depth and composition bias. Subsequent data analysis, including differential expression analysis, was conducted in R91 using respective Bioconductor packages92.

mRNA sequencing. Sequencing reads were aligned to the mouse reference genome from Gencode (vM25)93 using STAR aligner (v2.7.9a)94, and gene features were counted by using featureCounts v (2.0.3)95. The genes with low expression were filtered out using filterByExpr function with default settings from edgeR (v4.0.16)96 R package. Differential expression analyses were performed using edgeR’s voomLmFit97 function with sample quality weights (sample.weights=TRUE) and linear model “0 + group”, whereas group represents the combination of all experimental groups of interest. The experimental conditions and linear models used for each dataset are summarized below. Genes with adjusted p values below 0.05 were considered as differentially expressed. Gene enrichment analyses were performed by clusterProfiler (v4.10.1)98 R package using both over-representation analysis (ORA) and gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using differentially expressed genes and log-fold-change (logFC) ranked genes (n = 1,000,000), respectively. Gene permutation sets were retrieved from Gene Ontology (GO.db v3.18.0) and Reactome (reactome.db, v1.86.2) databases.

Smart-seq2 mRNA sequencing of murine blastomeres. Custom-made Smart-seq2 protocol was implemented as before74. Briefly, after thawing the plate, 1 µL of dNTP mix (10 mM), 0.1 µL of oligo-dT (100 µM, /5Biosg/AAGCAGTGGTATCAACGCAGAGTAC(T)30VN-3′) and 0.9 µl nuclease-free water were added to each well, and the lysis protocol was run when the samples were incubated at 72°C for 3 min in a thermocycler. Samples were then put on ice for at least 1 min. Next, 5.60 µL of reverse-transcription mix containing 0.25 µL of RNase I, 2 µL of 5× first-strand buffer, 2 µL of betaine (5 M), 0.06 µL of MgCl2 (1 M), 0.5 µL of DTT (100 mM), 0.5 µL of SuperScript III (200 U/µL), and 0.29 µl of nuclease-free water was added to each well and reverse transcription was carried out as follows: 42°C–90:00, 42°C hold, 42°C–12:20, 10 cycles (50°C–2:00, 42°C–2:00), 39°C–12:00, 70°C–15:00, 4°C hold. After the first 90 min of RT, 0.4 µL of 12,5 µM TSO (0.83 µM final concentration) was added to each reaction at room temperature. The plate was resealed, centrifuged for 1 min at 700×g, and placed back on the thermocycler to resume cycling from 42°C–12:20. After reverse transcription, 15 µL of cDNA enrichment PCR reaction mix containing 12.5 µL of 2× KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix, 0.25 µL of IS PCR primer (10 µM, /5Biosg/AAGCAGTGGTATCAACGCAGAGT-3′), and 2.25 µL of nuclease-free water was added to each well and cDNA enrichment PCR was performed as follows for 21 cycles: 98°C–3:00, 7 cycles (98°C–0:20, 60°C–4:00, and 72°C–6:00), 7 cycles (98°C–0:20, 64°C–0:30, and 72°C–6:00), and 7 cycles (98°C–0:20, 67°C–0:30, and 72°C–7:00), 72°C–10:00, 4°C hold. The cDNA purification was performed using AMPure XP beads at a ratio of 1:1 (Beckmann). For elution, Qiagen elution buffer (EB) was used. cDNA concentrations were measured using the Qubit 3.0 fluorometer according to the manufacturer’s protocol, and all cDNA samples were analyzed on Agilent Tapestation using the High Sensitivity DNA assay. Dual-indexed Illumina Nextera XT sequencing libraries were prepared using 25% of the recommended reaction volumes of Nextera XT components. All Nextera XT libraries were prepared using 125 pg of input cDNA for tagmentation, and were subsequently enriched for 12 PCR cycles, and purified using AMPure XP beads (Beckmann) at a sample:bead ratio of 0.6:1. Library concentrations were measured using Qubit 3.0 fluorometer, and the fragments were analyzed on the Agilent Tapestation using the High Sensitivity DNA assay. All libraries were individually normalized and diluted to a concentration of the pooled library to 5.4 ng/µL with an average size ~515 bp (16 nM). The libraries were sequenced on Illumina NextSeq 500 in a single-end 75-bp format (FC-404-2005, Illumina). Single-nuclei libraries were sequenced at an average depth of 3 million reads.

Male participants, sperm samples and analysis. The intervention study was approved by the Danish National Committee on Health Research Ethics (SJ-769), the Danish Data Protection Agency (REG-048-2019) and performed at the Fertility Clinic, Zealand University Hospital, Denmark77. The semen samples were collected from patients living with obesity (≥ 30 kg/m2) via masturbation following 2 days of abstinence. The sperm analyses were performed in the IVF laboratory in an authorized tissue establishment. The other semen samples were diluted with MHM-C (Fujifilm) and frozen immediately for further analysis. The semen samples were collected via masturbation following two days of abstinence, and the samples were analyzed a maximum of two to three hours after production. After liquefaction, ejaculate volume and sperm concentration (total, motile and progressive) were assessed using a microscope (Leica DM750). Sperm concentration was determined with a CellVision counting chamber (CellVision Technology, Heerhugowaard, the Netherlands). The sperm analyses were performed in the IVF laboratory in an authorized tissue establishment.

Study design and approvals. This prospective intervention study was conducted between May 2020 and April 2022 at the Fertility Clinic, Zealand University Hospital, Denmark. The primary outcomes have been published77. The study was approved by the Danish National Committee on Health Research Ethics (SJ-769), the Danish Data Protection Agency (REG-048-2019) and registered on the Clinical Trial website (www.ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT04721938). All participants provided written informed consent.

Primary adipocyte culture and transfection. Epididymal white adipose tissues (eWAT) from 6- to 8-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were removed, minced, and digested with pre-warmed collagenase media (500 U/mL collagenase type 2 (LS004183, Worthington) and 3.75 U/mL DNase I (10104159001, Sigma). Isolated cells were seeded in 6-well plates and grown in DMEM/Ham’s F12 medium (21331, Vendor: Gibco), supplemented with 0.1% Biotin/D-Pantothenate (33 mM/17 mM), 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 20% FBS. Until reaching 80% confluency, primary cells were induced by induction medium with 1 µM rosiglitazone, 850 nM insulin, 1 µM dexamethasone, 250 µM 3-isobutyl-1-methyl-xanthin (IBMX) and 10% FBS. Subsequently, the medium was changed every other day by a differentiation medium containing 1 µM rosiglitazone, 850 nM insulin and 10% FBS. 100 nM of Negative Control and mmu-let-7-d/e-5p mimics or LNA oligos targeting Dicer1 were reversely transfected using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at day 4 after induction. Completely differentiated cells were harvested at 7 days after induction for further analysis.

Plasmid design and dual luciferase assay. For the generation of reporter constructs, the specific region of murine Ago2, Dicer-1, Hif1an, Hk2, Cpt2, Crat, Pcx, Idh2, Sdha, Sdhaf3, Pdk2, Slc25a22 and Slc25a24 containing either wild-type (wt) or mutated (mut) let-7 binding sites was cloned behind the translation stop codon of the firefly-luciferase gene in pmirGLO Dual Luciferase vector using custom DNA oligos provided by IDT. Renilla luciferase coding in the same plasmid was used as a control reporter for normalization purposes. To report the miRNA activity in mammalian cells, HEK 293 cells were reversely transfected in 96-well plates with 60 ng DNA using the TransIT transfection reagent (mirus bio) for 3 days and forwardly transfected with let-7d/e-5p mimics for 2 days. HEK-293 cells were cultured in DMEM medium (21013, Gibco) supplemented with 5.6 mM L-glutamine, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 10% FBS. After 72-h vector transfection and 48-h miRNA mimics transfection, DLRAs (Promega) were performed. The relative activities of firefly luciferase, indicating the interaction between miRNA and the specific region of targeted mRNA were normalized by the activities of Renilla luciferase.

TaqMan assay and general qPCR. To quantify the levels of mature miRNAs, TaqMan MicroRNA Reverse-Transcription Kit (4366596, Thermo Fisher), TaqMan MicroRNA Assays and TaqMan Universal Master Mix II (4440042, Thermo Fisher) were applied according to manufacturer’s protocols. The level of mature hsa-miR-16 was used as an internal control in human samples. The relative expression of mature miRNA was calculated using a comparative method (2-∂∂CT) according to the ABI Relative Quantification Method.

Determination of OCRs and measurement of glycolytic activity. Primary adipocytes from epididymal SVF (1°eWA) were seeded into Agilent Seahorse XFe96 Bioanalyzer microplates. Induction and differentiation were performed as described above. After four days of differentiation, 16,000 per well mature adipocytes were re-seeded and transfected with LNA oligos targeting Dicer1 in DMEM/Ham’s F-12 medium plus 10% Fetal Bovine Serum, 1% P/S, 0.1% Biotin and 0.1% Pantothenic acid (Growth medium) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Seahorse measurement was conducted at day 7 from differentiation. For each seahorse plate, the corresponding calibration plate was prepared 24 hours prior to experiments using 200 µl XF Seahorse Calibrant Agilent per well. Corresponding media were prepared before the experiment and consisted of Assay Medium supplemented with 25 mM Glucose, 1 mM Glutamine, 2 mM Sodium Pyruvate, set to pH=7.4 and filtered sterile. The calibration plate possessed a cartridge having 4 pockets per well. Shortly before the measurement pocket A was filled with 20 µl 20 µM Oligomycin, pocket B with 22 µl 20 µM FCCP and pocket C with 25 µl 5 µM Antimycin A and Rotenone. One hour before measurements, plates were washed with 1× PBS and changed to 180 µl Assay Medium in a non-CO2 incubator at 37°C. Calibration was started using calibration plates, measuring O2 and pH LED Value/emission/Initial reference Delta for each well. All measurements started with measuring basal values, followed by injection of Oligomycin, FCCP, and Rotenone plus Antimycin A (Mito Stress Kit). Measurement parameters were: Mix 3 min, wait 0 min, measure 3 min with each reagent’s effect assessed within three consecutive measurement cycles with a total duration of 18 min per reagent injection.

Protein extraction and western blot analysis. After being washed once by PBS, the treated cells at harvest time were lysed by RIPA buffer supplemented with cOmplete and PhosSTOP and quantified by Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (23227, Thermo Fisher). Western blot analyses were carried out according to standard protocols with primary antibodies against COXIV (Cell Signaling Technologies #4850, 1:11,000 dilution), VDAC (Cell Signaling Technologies #4661, 1:11,000 dilution), HK2 (Cell Signaling Technologies #2897, 1:1,1000 dilution), SLC25A24 (Abcam Ab221120, 1:1000 dilution), CPT2 (Abcam Ab181114, 1:1,1000 dilution), CRAT (AP Proteintech #15170, 1:1000) and IDH2 (Cell Signaling Technologies #60322, 1:1,1000 dilution). Relative protein quantification was normalized by HSC70 (Santa Cruz sc-7298, 1:1000 dilution) or HSP90 (Cell Signaling Technologies #4877, 1:1000 dilution).

Access to reagents. All requests for data and reagent sharing should be directed to the corresponding author (janwilhelmkornfeld@bmb.sdu.dk).

Statistical analysis. Data were shown as mean ± standard error. One-way ANOVA and two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple comparisons test were used for statistical analysis in in vivo experiments. Significant differences between groups were noted in the figure legends, respectively.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

Huang et al. describe the intergenerational consequences of paternal obesity in mice by focusing on a diet-induced adipose-to-sperm miRNA axis involved in mitochondrial function.
The authors have compiled a significant amount of data which, while making the story compelling and interesting, leaves it difficult to follow. In general all my previous comments have been addressed and for this version, I do have the following general suggestions:
1. F1 glucose phenotypes - Still not clear to me what the n values mean, is it families? offspring? and - should the latter be the case - how have the offspring been selected?
2. F1 glucose phenotypes - given the slight but detectable differences in fasting glucose levels, it would be important to also show normalized glucose responses to understand whether the "glucose tolerance" phenotype is an exclusive function of the impaired fasting glycaemia
3. sperm smallRNA analysis - The authors have now included most of the smallRNA biotypes in the analysis, but I still miss the nuclear-encoded tRNAs, which have been implicated in paternal effects and might mirror miRNAs.
4. Single blastomere RNA-seq - What is the specific advantage and rationale of looking at single blastomeres, rather than running a bulk RNA-seq on single morula?
5. General writing - please go through the ms for typos (eg. offsprings) and correct figure indications.

### Reviewer 2

The revised manuscript is markedly improved and satisfactorily addresses most of the concerns raised in the previous round. Only two minor issues remain:
1. Overstatement of causality – The manuscript seems to imply that sperm-borne let-7 drives the entire inter-generational phenotype. Given that loss-of-function evidence is not presented, it would be more accurate to describe let-7 as “a contributing factor” rather than “the driver.” Please soften the wording accordingly.
2. Image clarity for western blots – Several immunoblots (notably CRAT in Fig. 5f and the blots in Fig. 5i, 5L) are blurry and difficult to interpret. Higher-resolution images would improve readability.

### Reviewer 3

The authors studied how paternal obesity influence offspring metabolic phenotypes. The authors found that sperm miRNAs, especially let-7 family members influence offspring by targeting mitochondrial function and TCA cycle crossing tissues, providing new insight into altered mitochondrial gene regulation and transcriptional rewiring during embryogenesis and in adult adipose tissue. While phenotypic and transcriptional changes are described, how sperm miRNA alterations mechanistically translate into tissue-specific mitochondrial dysfunction in offspring remains insufficiently elucidated. The observation that adipose tissue, but not other tissues like liver, shows transcriptional reversibility and mitochondrial regulation lacks mechanistic insight. The cause of adipose-specific sensitivity and the role of other tissues in glucose intolerance need clarification.
1.The study focuses on the short-term effect of metabolic changes in the offspring, but it lacks long-term follow-up to determine whether these effects last into later stages of life. A more comprehensive assay over time could provide insights into whether paternal obesity-induced epigenetic changes might contribute to age-related diseases such as type 2 diabetes or cardiovascular disease, which are common in individuals with a history of obesity.
2.The sperm miRNA profile was analyzed, but a broader and more comprehensive analysis could have been performed to explore the full spectrum of small non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs) that might be involved in transmitting the effects of paternal obesity. Exploring additional types of sncRNAs, such as piRNAs or other miRNAs, would help clarify whether let-7 alone is responsible for the observed effects or whether other regulatory RNAs also contribute to intergenerational inheritance.
3.The study focuses on a specific genetic background (C57BL/6N mice), which is a commonly used strain in metabolic research. However, it is unclear whether the observed intergenerational effects are common to other genetic backgrounds in mice.
4.The study mainly uses RNA sequencing and some histological analyses to assess the impact of paternal obesity. It will be great to show the context of mitochondrial morphology, such as electronic microscope, would provide a better understanding of the cellular and tissue-specific consequences of paternal obesity. It would be useful to compare the effects in other organs involved in metabolic regulation, such as muscle or pancreas, to demonstrate whether the effects are specific to adipose tissue or are more widespread.
5.Given that DICER1 is a global regulator of miRNA maturation, its knockdown could have widespread effects beyond mitochondrial biology. The specificity of this pathway in relation to mitochondrial impairment remains unclear.
6.The study uses LNA to knock down Dicer1. LNAs can have off-target interactions, especially when targeting highly conserved regions.
7.The idea that adipocyte-derived miRNAs are horizontally transferred to sperm via epididysomes remains unclear. No experiments, such as labeling, tracking of vesicle cargo, are conducted to demonstrate this cross-tissue miRNA transfer. These miRNA elevations could result from parallel responses to obesity rather than reflecting active cross-tissue transfer.
8.There are still other possibility from other epigenetic vectors such as DNA methylation, histone modifications that may also mediate intergenerational effects.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

We thank the reviewer for her/his encouraging remark and appreciation of the work performed to consolidate our findings. We do agree that a substantial set of data has been obtained and presented and have therefore restructured the paper to allow following the paper more easily. This involved presenting the data in a more natural order (for instance, but not limited to a side-by-side presentation of F0/F1 data to allow direct comparisons of metabolic and gene-regulatory effects).
Given the (intergenerational, multi organ, microRNA-mRNA datasets) ressource character of the paper, we decided to make the full dataset available to the community but, whenever possible, we have moved non-essential data to the Supplementary Information part of the paper for more clarity.
To not overcomplicate the paper, we have included the new data from the revision process in this rebuttal letter. We hope the letter can be made public in combination with the reviewers’ questions.
Question 1.
F1 glucose phenotypes - Still not clear to me what the n values mean, is it families? offspring? and - should the latter be the case - how have the offspring been selected?
Response 1.
We apologies for being unclear here: The n in the ipGTT represent the total number individual F1 mice. Per the 3 F1 groups we obtained 6-10 litters, and we randomly chose 1-2 mice per individual litter for subsequent metabolic and molecular analyses to end up with n=10 mice per each F1 group.
Question 2.
F1 glucose phenotypes - given the slight but detectable differences in fasting glucose levels, it would be important to also show normalized glucose responses to understand whether the "glucose tolerance" phenotype is an exclusive function of the impaired fasting glycaemia
Response 2.
We agree that the glucose excursion during an intraperitoneal GTT often reflects the basal (e.g.., 6h fasted) glycemia before the glucose challenge at T0. To account for this phenomenon, we had in our paper normalised glucose responses to individual glucose values at T0 in AUC calculations shown in Fig.S2a,b and as suggested by the reviewers. We have added the sentence ‘For area under the curve (AUC) calculations, we have normalised serum [Glu] values to [Glu, T0] of each animal to account for intra-animal variability in glucose responses and relative glucose responses’ to the Methods parts to avoid ambiguity.
Question 3.
Sperm smallRNA analysis - The authors have now included most of the smallRNA biotypes in the analysis, but I still miss the nuclear-encoded tRNAs, which have been implicated in paternal effects and might mirror miRNAs.
Response 3.
We agree that it is worthwhile to investigate nuclear-encoded tRNA fragments (tsRNAs) that have been described in the context of spermic alterations in obesity (PMID 26721685, 26721680). To our surprise, we did not detect significant trends in tsRNAs that were previously associated with epigenetic phenotypes, for instance Gly-GCC and Glu-CTC. We interpret this to be a potential consequence of the different diet feeding performed in aforementioned studies such as PMID 26721685 (19 versus 10% protein for control and our low-protein diet, LPD) or PMID 26721680 (similar HFD as our study, but different control diets) or different durations of diet feeding (PMID 26721685: 6-9 weeks LPD; PMID 26721680: 22 weeks HFD) compared to our study and, finally, depending on whether IVF was performed (PMID 26721685: Yes; PMID 26721680: No) which could all obfuscate obtaining similar results in our study.
Question 4.
Single blastomere RNA-seq - What is the specific advantage and rationale of looking at single blastomeres, rather than running a bulk RNA-seq on single morula?
Response 4.
When designing the scRNA-seq experiment we anticipated to detect inter-embryo / inter-blastomere differences as observed for mouse 2-/4-blastomere stage embryos (PMID: 25096407). To our surprise, the strong transcriptional effects following let-7 injection masked the intercellular differences. Thus, one might have a posteriori have resorted to bulk RNA-seq on single morulae, as suggested, but we think that providing the single-cell resolved data to be appropriate at this point.
Question 5.
General writing - please go through the ms for typos (eg. offsprings) and correct figure indications.
Response 5:
We apologize for the remaining typographical errors that were also overlooked using a spelling program. We manually went through the paper and corrected mistakes with a focus on genitive case.
Reply:
We are happy to learn that this reviewer appreciates our additional analysis and that we were able to address most of his/her concerns.
Question 6.
Overstatement of causality – The manuscript seems to imply that sperm-borne let-7 drives the entire inter-generational phenotype. Given that loss-of-function evidence is not presented, it would be more accurate to describe let-7 as “a contributing factor” rather than “the driver.” Please soften the wording accordingly.
Response 6.
We agree that overstatements compromise the impact of our work and have throughout the manuscript mitigated statements not backed up by data. We also appreciate that, while spermic let-7 has been associated with intergenerational epigenetic effects in obese rodents (PMID: 26977389) and in this study, other sncRNA have been described (miR-19, mt-tRNAs and mt-tsRNAs, reviewed in PMID: 32415866) that might contribute to the intergenerational effects on glucose metabolism and mitochondrial function that we described. Whilst these studies did not perform sncRNA injection experiments, some of them have demonstrated sperm-oocyte transfer (PMID: 38839949). Thus, we throughout the paper we referred to let-7 as a contributing factor and not driver of heritable effects.
Question 7.
Image clarity for western blots – Several immunoblots (notably CRAT in Fig. 5f and the blots in Fig. 5i, 5L) are blurry and difficult to interpret. Higher-resolution images would improve readability.
Response 7.1:
We acknowledge that the quality of Western Blot analyses can be improved and the low affinity of antibodies targeting mitochondrial ETC / TCA components constitutes an important limitation, particularly when interrogating lipid-rich tissues like fat. Despite several attempts, the quality for CRAT could not be improved. Thus, despite our luciferase data suggesting CRAT to be targeted by let-7 in HEK cells, we could not adress this functional interaction in adipocytes (Fig.5f). Given this, and the fact that we do not further pursue the role of CRAT in adipocytes, we omitted CRAT Western Blots. More limiting is the poor quality of DICER1 Western Blots. Post-transcriptional silencing of DICER1 by let-7 is central to our paper, and despite this interaction being shown in other cellular contexts such as cancer cells (PMID: 18700235). DICER1 Western Blot remains cumbersome due to the large size of the protein (217kDa) thus inefficacy of transfer as well as its poor (tryptic) digest which leads to DICER1 peptides not being present in proteomic datasets, also ours.
Response 7.2:
Although not explicitly asked for by the reviewers, we unsolicitedly aimed to strengthen the functional interaction between let-7 and reduced DICER1 in adipocytes, and to address the point of hitherto relying only on let-7 loss-of-function gain-of-function experiments, we have additionally performed let-7d/e inhibition using locked nucleic acid (LNA) inhibitors in primary adipocytes. As expected, densitometric quantification revealed that loss of let-7 increased levels of DICER1 protein, but not other that of other predicted let-7d/e targets (HK2, CPT2). The fact that both let-7 gain-of-function (old version of the paper), but also loss-of-function (included in this rebuttal letter) antagonise and restore DICER1 protein, we are confident regarding our major claim of functionally linking let-7 abundances to post-transcriptional repression of DICER1.
Reply:
We thank the reviewer for his/her points and for thoroughly assessing our work. We agree with the reviewer and the editor that these points warrant a detailed analysis of our sncRNA data, of testing the possibility of horizontal let-7 transfer and additional experiments regarding the function of DICER1 in mitochondrial regulation in adipocytes. We hope that by our extensive additional experiments we have addressed the reviewer’s concerns and hope that our manuscript of sufficiently quality for publication in Nature Communications.
Question 8:
The study focuses on the short-term effect of metabolic changes in the offspring, but it lacks long-term follow-up to determine whether these effects last into later stages of life. A more comprehensive assay over time could provide insights into whether paternal obesity-induced epigenetic changes might contribute to age-related diseases such as type 2 diabetes or cardiovascular disease, which are common in individuals with a history of obesity.
Response 8:
We agree that analysing the effect of time that F1 phenotypes need to unfold is an important consideration. In our initial paper we chose to interrogate F1 metabolism after 21 weeks of LFD feeding to align with the duration of F0 diet interventions. We could not extend the duration of HFD/LFD feeding beyond 24 weeks of age due to welfare considerations and ethical approvals that limit the duration of HFD feeding in F0, but also as we consider conducting a full (F1) ageing study beyond the scope of this paper.
As we were nonetheless interested in testing whether F1 phenotypes occurred earlier than at 24 weeks of age (TP2), we analysed F1 mice also at 15 weeks of age (TP1, data hitherto not shown in the paper). In contrast to F1 mice analysed and sacrificed at TP2, no alterations in glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity evidenced by ipGTT/ipITT can be observed in male and female mice at TP1. Thus, our data suggest that F1 effects require a time window of >12 weeks post-weaning and LFD feeding to unfold, and/or an additional F1 HFD burden (PMID: 26974008).
Question 9.
The sperm miRNA profile was analyzed, but a broader and more comprehensive analysis could have been performed to explore the full spectrum of small non-coding RNAs (sncRNAs) that might be involved in transmitting the effects of paternal obesity. Exploring additional types of sncRNAs, such as piRNAs or other miRNAs, would help clarify whether let-7 alone is responsible for the observed effects or whether other regulatory RNAs also contribute to intergenerational inheritance.
Response 9:
We acknowledged the importance of addressing the point of whether other sncRNAs beyond let-7 contribute to epigenetic phenotypes, which has also been raised by Reviewer 2 (see rebuttal to Q6). To address the contribution of other sncRNAs than microRNAs in somatic tissues (eWAT), we quantified cumulative counts and unique no. of sequences sncRNA biotypes across F0/F1 eWAT and F0 sperm using the same computational workflow for all three datasets. Here, comparison was performed on a sequence level, annotating them to Ensembl’s non-coding and coding RNA references, as well as piRBase and miRBase to investigate a broad spectrum of biotypes.
As described in the literature (PMID: 31681757) we observe the highest variation between small RNA biotypes in sperm, whereas eWAT exhibited the lowest variation (limited to expression of microRNAs and piRNAs for F0 eWAT). We think this argues against performing an even more thorough analysis of non-microRNA sncRNA biotypes in F0/F1 adipose tissue. This would only be meaningful in our eyes for piRNAs, but these are functionally connected to transposon silencing and germline maintenance, whereas an implication of piRNAs in (multi/inter)-generational epigenetic memory has only been described in lower organisms (PMID: 22738725). Finally, while we appreciate the potential implication of other sncRNAs in intergenerational crosstalk (notably 5’ tsRNA fragments) tsRNA were not differentially expressed in eWAT. Thus, we opted not to perform microinjection experiments using tsRNAs, we think that functionally delineating their contribution, i.e., by additional embryonic microinjection experiments (and scRNA-seq) as done for mmu-let-7d/e is beyond the scope of the study. Furthermore, as described in Q6, we have toned down the statement that let7 drives all the effects to "are a factor" of the effect.
Question 10.
The study focuses on a specific genetic background (C57BL/6N mice), which is a commonly used strain in metabolic research. However, it is unclear whether the observed intergenerational effects are common to other genetic backgrounds in mice.
Response 10.
We think that this is an excellent point and repeating these studies in other (obesity-resistent) genetic background such as Sv/129 or outbred strains would add to the rigor of our findings. Given that let-7c has been described in an intergenerational rodent obesity study that used non-syngenic rats as model (PMID: 26977389), we think repeating our study in another extensive mouse cohort does not warrant the amount of resources needed to do so.
Question 11a.
The study mainly uses RNA sequencing and some histological analyses to assess the impact of paternal obesity. It will be great to show the context of mitochondrial morphology, such as electron microscope, which would provide a better understanding of the cellular and tissue-specific consequences of paternal obesity.
Response 11b.
In addition to the transcriptomic and histological analyses presented in the study, our data further indicate alterations in mitochondrial morphology in epididymal white adipocytes of obese fathers. Specifically, we observed that paternal obesity (F0 HF) leads to smaller and more irregularly shaped and fragmented mitochondria compared to F0 LF/F0 HF-LF, likely reflecting the TEM manifestations of mitochondrial dysfunction that were published recently in Nature Metabolism (PMID 38286821) and before (PMID: 16501941, 15520860). Thus, these morphological changes support the downregulation of mitochondria-related pathways identified in our multi-omics analyses.
Question 11b.
It would be useful to compare the effects in other organs involved in metabolic regulation, such as muscle or pancreas, to demonstrate whether the effects are specific to adipose tissue or are more widespread.
Response 11b.
We appreciate that our current analysis which focuses on transcriptional effects in mitochondrial genes might be (too) limited by investigating mitochondrial gene expression only in liver and adipose tissue. We thus designed qPCR primers for genes deregulated in obese F0 and F1 adipose tissue and measured the expression of these genes in other F0 and F1 metabolic tissues:
Importantly, when interrogating expression of mitochondrial gene expression(mtCox2), nuclearly-encoded mitochondrial proteins (Tfam, Cox5b, Sdhb, Ndufa1, Ndufs1, Ndufa8, Atp5a1, Cox6a2, Atpaf2, Atp5if1, Atp5g3) and regulators of nuclear expression of mitochondrial proteins (Nrf2) in the heart, a tissue dependent on oxidative respiration, kidney and skeletal muscle, two organs important for glucose regulation, we did not observe alterations in mitochondrial genes, but also not of membrane calcium-transporting ATPase 2 (Atp2b2). We conclude that the alterations in glucose tolerance and systemic alterations in metabolites indicative of impaired mitochondrial function that we reported for F0 HFD exposed animals (and F1 progeny) triggers mitochondrial dysfunction predominantly in epididymal white adipose tissue, but not in the other metabolic tissues that we investigated. We aimed to isolate RNA from pancreati which we isolated but unfortunately the RNA integrity was insufficient to perform qPCR analysis.
Question 12.
Given that DICER1 is a global regulator of miRNA maturation, its knockdown could have widespread effects beyond mitochondrial biology. The specificity of this pathway in relation to mitochondrial impairment remains unclear.
Response 12.
Although the role of adipose DICER1 in mitochondrial gene regulation has been explored in the context of organismal ageing and calorie restriction (PMID: 27241713), a thorough investigation of the metabolic roles of DICER1 in mature adipocytes has not been performed yet, so this is a valid point that we wanted to address with additional experiments. To address the role of DICER1 selectively in adipocytes, we resorted to a new cellular model (Rocha et al. Unpublished, PMID: 33268375) that ablates DICER1 in immortalised, mature adipocytes of subcutaneous origin in a Tamoxifen-inducible manner (DICER1-KO cells). Using this system, we investigated mitochondrial respiration using Seahorse and found that, as seen using LNA-mediated DICER1 knockdown, that genetic deletion of DICER1 also blunted oxygen consumption, indicating reduced mitochondrial numbers and/or function.
Question 13.
The study uses LNA to knock down Dicer1. LNAs can have off-target interactions, especially when targeting highly conserved regions.
Response 13.
We acknowledge the limitations of LNA-mediated DICER1 knockdown and risk of off-target effects, particularly when using short LNA GapmeR. As shown in point 12, we validated the mitochondrial (respiratory) defects of inducible DICER1 knockouts in mature adipocytes (DICER1-KO cells) and in adipose tissue of conditional DICER1-KO mice, reenforcing the functional connection between DICER1 deficiency and transcriptional mitochondrial impairment across several (KD, KO) orthologous cellular and mouse models.
Question 14.
The idea that adipocyte-derived miRNAs are horizontally transferred to sperm via epididysomes remains unclear. No experiments, such as labeling, tracking of vesicle cargo, are conducted to demonstrate this cross-tissue miRNA transfer. These miRNA elevations could result from parallel responses to obesity rather than reflecting active cross-tissue transfer.
Response 14.
We think this is an excellent point which we address using new data from our lab and additional re-analyses of public data. To address this question comprehensively, we used the Dicer1-AdcKO mouse line to define and measure ’sentinel’ microRNAs that are absent from KO fat and tracked their regulation in sperm (R14.1) and addressed trafficking of let-7 isoforms using public data (R14.2).
Response 14.1 Transfer of mature ’sentinel’ microRNAs from adipose tissue to sperm
To get insight into the transfer of adipocyte-derived microRNAs into spermatozoa, we used the adipocyte-specific DICER1-AdcKO model to deplete microRNAs in adipocytes as described by us and others (PMID: 22958919, 26900752, 24983316). In this context testing let-7 is not ideal these microRNAs are ubiquitous and highly abundant in circulation. Thus, DICER1-AdcKO evoked loss of let-7 in adipocytes might not meaningfully reduce sperm let-7 level; particularly considering compensatory mechanisms that we observed in other settings.
Instead, we focussed on microRNAs that are known to be exchanged by microvesicular (MV) transfer (PMID: 39285292), are highly abundant in fat, and have in the past been proven to be adipocyte DICER KO-sensitive miRNAs. miR-16-5p and miR-92a-3p fulfill this criterion and accordingly were repressed in adipose tissue of DICER1-AdcKO mice, whereas adipocyte DICER insensitive miRNAs such as miR-193b-5p and miR-99b-5p were unaffected by DICER1 knockout.
Response 14.2 Transfer of let-7 isoforms from testicular cell types to sperm:
Given that we only validated horizontal transfer of microRNAs between fat tissue and sperm by determining the exchange miR-16-5p/92a-3p, but not let7 (which was also not directly affected by DICER1 KO), we next specifically addressed the transfer of let-7 isoforms between testicular cell types and sperm: For this, we re-analysed data from a study that used testicular germ cell (GC)-specific (Dgcr8fl/fl; Stra8-iCre+/-) and epididymes (Epi) specific (Dgcr8fl/fl; Defb41-iCre). Knockout of Dgcr8 was used to achieve microRNA loss in GC and Epi, respectively. Following microRNA depletion in GC/Epi, sRNA-seq in sperm was performed to delineate the cellular origin of spermic microRNA and possibility for horizontal transfer of microRNAs (including let-7) between testicular somatic and germ cells. Intriguingly, Dgcr8 KO in epididymis did not cause a reduction in most microRNAs including let-7 in sperm (top), whereas deficiency of microRNAs in testicular germ cells did. This suggested to us that provisioning of let-7 to sperm must happen early during sperm formation, as deleting maturation of let-7 and most other microRNAs secreted from the cauda epididymes are insufficient to change sperm microRNA payloads.
Response 15.
We acknowledge the existence of other gene-regulatory (chromatin based) modalities that have been reported to affect intergenerational traits. As our focus was on specifically investigating sncRNA which (in contrast to DNA methylation and histone PTM) have the capacity to be physically exchanged between tissues and cells, and because we here demonstrate that certain microRNA even undergo horizontal transfer between adipocytes and sperm (response to question 14), we consider performing additional omics beyond the scope of this paper but will include this shortcoming in the the discussion.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.
